items.prompt: Distinguish constructive and destructive waves by their energy, form and effect on the beach.
items.canonical_answer: Constructive waves are low-energy, low waves with a long wavelength that break infrequently and spill, so the swash is stronger than the backwash and material is built up on the beach. Destructive waves are high-energy, high and steep waves that break frequently and plunge, so the backwash is stronger than the swash and material is dragged off the beach.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the energy difference: constructive low energy, whereas destructive high energy.
1 mark for a difference in form: height/steepness, wavelength, frequency or spilling versus plunging breakers.
1 mark for the difference in swash/backwash balance linked to its effect: build-up versus removal of beach material.

context.situation: Original self-contained Geography resource; invented numbers and scenarios are synthetic, not real-place measurements.

items.canonical_answer:
Regime A is constructive: swash moves 30 units up the beach but backwash returns only 18, and the upper profile builds up. items.prompt: Describe the swash/backwash sequence that produces longshore drift.
items.canonical_answer: Waves driven by the prevailing wind approach the beach at an angle, so the swash carries material diagonally up the beach. The backwash returns it straight down the slope under gravity. Repeated swash and backwash move the material in a zigzag along the coast.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the first step: wind-driven waves approach at an angle, giving diagonal swash.
1 mark for the next step: backwash returns straight down the slope under gravity.
1 mark for the result: repeated movements give net zigzag transport along the coast.

items.prompt:
![Plan of a north-south beach with the sea to the west, waves approaching from the south-west, and a marked grain moved from origin O to positions 1 to 4](../assets/images/ITEM-6137-1.5-029-INTERP-question.png)

Describe the net direction shown in this plan: sea west, land east, north-eastward swash and westward downslope return, repeated from the marked origin O. Use its north arrow and sediment path.
items.canonical_answer:
Swash moves the grain north-eastward up the beach and backwash returns it westward downslope, giving a zigzag path. Each cycle leaves the grain farther north: positions 1 to 4 lie north of O. The repeated path therefore retains a northward component, so net drift is northward for the observed interval.

items.prompt: How far do you agree that the groyne succeeds for both communities? Drift is northward; sand accumulates south of the groyne while the northern neighbouring beach narrows. Judge beach protection across both frontages.

items.prompt: How far do you agree that gabions are a suitable defence for this frontage? items.canonical_answer: Agree to a large extent. Gabions are cheap and quick to build, and their rock-filled baskets absorb some wave energy, which suits a short frontage with moderate waves and a small budget. items.prompt: How far do you agree that beach nourishment is the best way to keep this tourist beach wide? items.canonical_answer: Agree to a large extent. Nourishment adds sand directly, so it widens the beach and keeps a natural sandy surface that tourists use, and a seawall is both unaffordable and unable to rebuild beach width. A supplied safe survey compares beaches A and B. H1: A has a steeper overall surveyed profile than B. H2: A is wider than B at the comparable reference level. A profile data (distance m, height m): (0,0), (10,0.5), (20,1.5), (30,3). B: (0,0), (10,0.3), (20,1). Heights were worked out from the field angle and distance readings. Width repeats: A 30,32,31 m; B 20,22,21 m. The profile plot must use the supplied axes: distance 0–30 m, height 0–3 m. Use provided data; do not enter hazardous water.
(a) Name the instrument used to measure a beach-slope angle. [1]
(b) Describe the sequence producing longshore drift. [3]
(c) Name two pieces of equipment, other than a clinometer, used to survey a beach profile. [2]
(d) Calculate A’s overall gradient as a ratio with both distances in metres. [3]
(e) Describe the A/B profile pattern using values. [3]
(f) What conclusion about H1 is supported, with a limitation? [3]
(g) What conclusion about H2 is supported, with a limitation? [3]
(h) Design a repeatable profile procedure using the same reference conditions. [3]
(i) Describe how distance and angle readings would be recorded consistently. [3]
(j) Complete the field-record headings for the two variables needed for each profile segment, including units. [2]
(k) Plot A’s four supplied points on the provided axes. [2]
(l) Explain why comparable tide/reference conditions matter. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Clinometer. (b) In this wind-generated wave model, waves approach at an angle, so swash moves material diagonally up the beach; backwash returns it straight downslope; repeated cycles produce net alongshore displacement. (c) Ranging poles and a tape measure. (d) Vertical/horizontal = 3/30 = 0.1, equivalent to gradient 1:10. (e) A rises 3 m over 30 m; B 1 m over 20 m, making A steeper overall in these surveys. (f) H1 is supported by 1:10 versus 1:20; these are sampled profiles, not every place/date. (g) All supplied A widths exceed B, supporting H2 for the comparable measurements; the sample does not establish all-season widths. (h) Fixed start, defined shore-normal line and consistent pole/segment method under approved safe comparable conditions. (i) Record positions, distances and signed angles with consistent pole reference heights and units, retaining repeats or errors transparently. (j) Segment distance (m); slope angle (degrees). (k) Correct coordinates are (0,0),(10,0.5),(20,1.5),(30,3), connected in order. (l) Water level changes apparent width/reference positions, so comparable conditions reduce a timing/measurement confound.

![Beach A profile plotted and field-record headings completed](../assets/images/ITEM-6137-1.5-P04-VIS-6137-1.5-05-answer.png)
marking_guidance: (a) 1 A for clinometer; (b) 3 A for wind-driven oblique swash, backwash straight downslope and repeated net movement; (c) 2 A, one each for ranging poles and tape measure (accept compass for transect direction).
(d) 3 B: method vertical/horizontal in equal units, 3/30 simplification, correct 1:10 ratio. (e) 3 B: A values, B values and the comparative interpretation.

(f) 3 C: supported hypothesis H1 conclusion, comparative gradient evidence and evaluation of sampled-profile limitations. (g) 3 C: supported hypothesis H2 conclusion, repeated width evidence and limited-period coverage.
(h) 3 D: reference/line, consistent equipment/segment procedure, approved safe/comparable conditions. (i) 3 D: traceable position record, consistent distance/angle procedure, signs/units/repeats.

(j) 2 D: one per correct variable heading with unit. (k) 2 D: accurate supplied-coordinate plotting and appropriate ordered connection on the supplied axes; no credit merely for rewriting the list. (l) 2 D: reason linking tide to width/reference and the resulting comparability.

(l) Explain why a larger sample alone does not fix biased selection. [2]

(a) Attrition. (b) Transported particles collide, corners/fragments are removed and particles can become smaller/rounder. (c) Size and roundness/shape. (d) (18+20+22)/3 = 20 mm. (e) Mean size rises 20→30→40 mm, while rounded counts rise then fall 0→1→0. (f) H1 is supported at these sites; source differences and the small/date-specific sample limit a broader claim. (h) State a start and regular interval, apply an unbiased fixed local selection rule and predeclare treatment when no eligible pebble is present. (h) 3 D: start/interval, consistent eligible selection, predeclared absence rule. (i) 3 D: axis/units, shared shape scale, position-linked record.

H2: recovered displacement increases in every successive trial. Trials 1–5 record +2,+4,+1,−1 m, and not recovered. (a) Name the net alongshore sediment-transport process. [1]
(b) Describe its swash/backwash sequence. [3]

(g) What conclusion on H2 is supported, with a limitation? [3]
(h) Design repeated movement observations with a defined reference and safe approved method. [3]
(i) Describe a record that distinguishes recovery, zero and unknown positions. [3]
(j) Complete the totals for recovered and unrecovered trials. [2]
(k) Plot recovered signed displacements on supplied axes, leaving non-recovery distinct. [2]
(l) Explain why replacing non-recovery with zero could mislead. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Longshore drift. (b) In this wind-generated wave model, waves approach at an angle, so swash carries sediment diagonally up the beach; return backwash moves downslope; repetition produces net alongshore movement. (c) Distance and direction. (d) (2+4+1−1)/4 = +1.5 m, northward. (e) Three northward records and one southward record; values do not increase steadily. (f) H1 is supported by the positive mean among recovered observations; missing trial 5 and short coverage limit the inference. (g) H2 is not supported: +4 falls to +1 and then −1; unknown trial 5 cannot repair the documented decreases. (h) State origin/direction and equal duration, repeat the approved observation method and retain safety/environmental constraints. (i) Record trial/time, position or signed distance/direction and recovery status; zero is a known unchanged position while unknown is missing. (j) Four recovered, one unrecovered. (k) Plot (1,2),(2,4),(3,1),(4,−1); mark trial 5 as missing separately. (l) Unknown position could have moved either way; inventing zero changes the mean and may distort the decision.

marking_guidance: (a) 1 A for longshore drift; (b) 3 A for wind-driven oblique swash, backwash straight downslope and repeated net alongshore movement; (c) 2 A for distance and direction.
(d) 3 B: signed-sum method 6/4, +1.5 result, m/north direction. (e) 3 B for the positive majority, negative exception and non-increasing sequence using the data.

(f) 3 C: hypothesis H1 conclusion for recovered data, positive-mean evidence, evaluation of missing/short-period limitations. (g) 3 C: hypothesis H2 rejection conclusion, documented decreases and correct treatment of unknown trial.
(h) 3 D: fixed reference, equal repeated interval/method, safe approved constraints. (i) 3 D: trial-linked measurements, direction-aware values, separate recovery/zero/unknown record.

(j) 2 D for four recovered and one missing. (k) 2 D for correct signed plotting and distinct missing-data treatment on supplied axes. (l) 2 D for the unknown-versus-zero reason and its effect on estimates/conclusions.

![Survey layout: fixed reference post, shore-normal transect, poles, clinometer, tape and record sheet](../assets/images/ITEM-6137-1.5-046-PROC-question.png)

![Blank paired before-and-after axes for mean width (0 to 35 m) at reaches U, D and C](../assets/images/ITEM-6137-1.5-P07-VIS-6137-1.5-08-question.png)

A hypothetical groyne investigation compares a southern updrift reach U, northern downdrift reach D and a reference reach C. Repeated surveys use comparable tide/reference conditions. H1: U gains more width than C. H2: D does not narrow. Mean widths before→after are D 18→10 m and C 20→19 m. U’s mean width before was 20 m; its three after readings are 29, 30 and 31 m. Wave/tracer observations support northward transport. Use supplied before/after plotting axes: reach U,D,C and width 0–35 m.
(a) Name the uprush after wave breaking. [1]
(b) Describe how a groyne can affect longshore sediment supply. [3]
(c) Name two pieces of equipment needed to measure beach width along a fixed transect. [2]
(d) Using U’s mean after width from part (j), calculate its percentage width increase, with the before width as denominator. [3]
(e) Describe the before/after contrasts across the three reaches. [3]
(f) What conclusion on H1 is supported, with a limitation? [3]
(g) What conclusion on H2 is supported, with a limitation? [3]
(h) Design a repeatable survey to test future width changes, including a suitable comparison. [3]
(i) Describe how to control or record tide/reference and transect differences. [3]
(j) Complete U’s mean after width and its unit from the three readings. [2]
(k) Plot the before/after widths for U,D,C on the supplied axes. [2]
(l) Explain why the reference reach helps but does not prove a unique cause. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Swash. (b) A groyne intercepts some alongshore material, encouraging updrift accumulation and potentially reducing onward supply. (c) A tape measure and ranging poles (or a compass to keep the transect direction). (d) (30−20)/20×100 = 50%. (e) U gains 10 m, D loses 8 m, C loses 1 m. (f) H1 is supported by U +10 versus C −1, but reaches may differ in other controls. (g) H2 is rejected by D’s measured 8 m narrowing; the change is compatible with reduced supply but does not alone prove the groyne is its sole cause. (h) Fixed comparable transects on both sides and at a justified reference, repeated over relevant dates with a stated width datum. (i) Use the same fixed starts/directions and comparable level conditions, recording timing and wave/context differences. (j) (29+30+31)/3 = 30 m. (k) U bars 20/30, D 18/10, C 20/19 with a clear before/after distinction. (l) The reference indicates wider change, but local differences and other inputs can remain, limiting unique causal attribution.

![Annotated repeatable survey procedure](../assets/images/ITEM-6137-1.5-046-PROC-answer.png)

![Paired bars: U 20 to 30 m, D 18 to 10 m, C 20 to 19 m](../assets/images/ITEM-6137-1.5-P07-VIS-6137-1.5-08-answer.png)
marking_guidance: (a) 1 A for swash; (b) 3 A for interception, updrift effect and potential onward-supply effect; (c) 2 A, one each for tape measure and ranging poles (accept compass).
(d) 3 B: correct increase/before method, substitution 10/20×100 and 50% result. (e) 3 B for the three correctly interpreted changes.
(f) 3 C: supported hypothesis H1 conclusion, U/C evidence and evaluation of comparability limitations. (g) 3 C: hypothesis H2 rejection conclusion, D change and qualified causal interpretation.
(h) 3 D: spatial comparison, fixed datum/transects, repeat plan. (i) 3 D: location consistency, level/time handling, contextual record.
(j) 2 D for mean 30 and unit m. (k) 2 D for accurate paired plotting and distinguishable before/after presentation. (l) 2 D for the wider-change reason and remaining local-confound limitation.
